claims.claim: Krege's 2000 German retranslation deliberately re-differentiated Tolkien's registers, modernising the hobbits' speech into late-1990s German against a biblical high style for Elves and human nobility, where Carroux (1969-70) had used one unified style.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: German critics judged that Krege took too many liberties in a translator-centred approach unsuited to Tolkien, and the 2012 edition reverted the most controversial decisions.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Linguist Rainer Nagel found that Krege corrects Carroux's errors but often overshoots his target.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Carroux treated the source with enormous respect and a unified linguistic style, and Tolkien was delighted with her work apart from the poems.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege's rendering of Sam's 'Master' as 'Chef' (boss) was criticised as misrepresenting a rural gardener's relation to his employer, and the September 2012 revision removed it.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege spanned registers from sixteenth-century Bible German to colloquial speech but anchored them to 1990s German rather than the 1940s of the original, and many readers rejected the differentiation as overdrawn.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege's 'unermüdlich wedelndem Laubwerk' for 'ever-moving leaves' was attacked for distorting the symbol of transience and Elvish departure.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)

claims.claim: The German film dubbing kept Carroux's version rather than Krege's, visible in the third film's title remaining 'Die Rückkehr des Königs'.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — Übersetzungen (de.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege aimed to reproduce Tolkien's speech registers from Biblical language to 1940s British colloquialism, against what he saw as Carroux's uniform, artificially folksy German.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege's 1998 Hobbit restored the poems Scherf had cut but interpreted sentences freely and admitted anachronisms such as 'Hurricane'.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Krege said he wanted to translate as Tolkien would write in 1999, directly from Westron into German.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)

claims.claim: Krege's slang such as 'Penner' (bum) and 'Dalli Dalli' (hurry up) dated quickly and read as anachronistic.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)

claims.claim: Krege replaced the historical deferential 'Ihr' with modern 'Sie', creating an odd modern formality in a medieval society.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)

claims.claim: Editor Ulrike Killer defended Krege's version as timely for the films and preferable to a monochromatic and dated Carroux.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)

claims.claim: Lisa Kuppler's 2012 revision preserved Krege's stylistic approach but corrected orthography and restored the traditional address for Frodo.
claims.source: Wolfgang Krege (Ardapedia)

claims.feature: translator's theory of colour and tempo
claims.claim: Krege (Tolkien Times, August 2000) set out to give the text its own life in the German language's room for 'Farbe, Tempo, Kontrasten'.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)

claims.claim: Krege argued the old faithful translation inevitably makes the expression a little paler, the tempo slower and the style more uniform; Weinreich rejects 'paler' as nonsense but grants the rest.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: ein wenig blasser, das Tempo langsamer

claims.claim: Weinreich argues 'Master' and 'Sir' express Sam's working-class standing against Frodo's gentry more than an employment relation, so Carroux's 'Herr' is correct and Krege's 'Chef' means what 'Boss' would mean, which is not in Tolkien.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)
claims.quote: das steht bei Tolkien aber nicht

claims.claim: In the Aglarond sentence Carroux keeps Tolkien's 'make ... bend' construction at some cost to fluency, while Krege's 'Kräuter' for 'weed' is botanically wrong where 'Wasserpflanzen' is right.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)

claims.feature: error density in a modernised text
claims.claim: A Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft project team found hundreds of smaller and larger errors in Krege's translation, which Weinreich attributes to a rush job ahead of the Jackson films.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)

claims.claim: Weinreich prefers Krege's 'Kunde' to Carroux's 'Bursche' for Farmer Maggot's 'fellow' (the Black Rider) because the modern word carries the original's ambivalence.
claims.source: Anmerkungen zu den deutschen Übersetzungen des HdR (Frank Weinreich, polyoinos)

claims.claim: Held's thesis finds Carroux foreignises through the archaic deferential 'Ihr' and at places awkward syntax, so that to a German reader her text may read like a translation from Middle High German.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Krege uses modern German but preserves archaism where Tolkien contrasts archaic and modern speech, for example when Théoden first meets the hobbits at Isengard.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Krege's 'modern' words such as 'Halunke' no longer read as modern in 2021, while Nagel in 2004 objected to 'speziell' as ruining Butterbur's simple speech.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Nagel, quoted by Held, holds that Krege approached the book as a modernisation of Tolkien's text for what he believed was a new generation of readers.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Tolkien's Butterbur speaks an old-fashioned rural dialect; Krege gives him vernacular ('Dalli, dalli!' for 'Double sharp!') while Carroux translates verbatim ('Schneller, schneller!').
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Krege repeatedly introduces German idioms where the English had none, turning Gandalf's 'I shall roast him' into 'wasch' ich ihm den Kopf' with oral contractions in a written letter, which loses the literal threat and alters Gandalf.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Held concludes Krege is domesticating and dynamically equivalent while Carroux is foreignising and formally equivalent, so Krege's version shifts character perception more (Gollum and the Black Riders more or less animalistic, Galadriel's title and standing).
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Both translations keep Tolkien's foreignised compound 'sister-son' as 'Schwestersohn' rather than 'Neffe'.
claims.source: Alexander Held, Lost in Translation: How the perception of Characters changes in the German Translations of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings (MA thesis, Waterloo/Mannheim 2021)

claims.claim: Nagel's chapter reports Krege defending his version as 'assimilating the alien' where Carroux merely rendered the text, and concludes that Krege's language for younger readers sometimes fails to convey the voice the author intended.
claims.source: Review: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Mythopoeic Society)

claims.claim: Honegger shows Tolkien's 'thou' carries five functions (poetry, archaism, contempt, emotion, familiarity) that German du/Sie and French tu/vous cannot reproduce.
claims.source: Review: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Mythopoeic Society)

claims.claim: Stenström notes the Swedish 'älvor' for elves imports unwanted fairy connotations.
claims.source: Review: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Mythopoeic Society)

claims.claim: Nagel's Prancing Pony example shows Krege shifting Butterbur from an elderly innkeeper to a younger colloquial speaker, e.g. 'Penner' where Carroux had 'Faultier'.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Cormarë 6) — Nagel and Honegger chapters (epdf mirror)

claims.claim: Nagel argues Krege's modernisation paradoxically creates a new uniformity by narrowing vocabulary range and simplifying archaic constructions.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Cormarë 6) — Nagel and Honegger chapters (epdf mirror)

claims.claim: Honegger explains that Tolkien equated Rohirric with Old English to keep linguistic distance while suggesting kinship, a choice translators cannot easily mirror.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien: Text and Film (Cormarë 6) — Nagel and Honegger chapters (epdf mirror)

claims.feature: reader verdict: register equated with ours
claims.claim: SpacePub readers objected that 'Chef' equates the hobbits' social circumstances with ours and that 'Penner', 'Imbissbude' and 'Stuss erzählen' break immersion, while supporters praised readability and regional differentiation of hobbit, Rohirric and Elvish speech.
claims.source: Der Herr der Ringe — die neue Übersetzung beurteilt (SpacePub forum archive)

claims.claim: In the SF-Fan thread all twelve poll votes called the Krege translation an absolute failure, and one reader said the Middle-earth medieval atmosphere was gone, replaced by soap-opera modernity.
claims.source: Herr der Ringe — Krege-Übersetzung (SF-Fan forum)
claims.quote: die Stimmung ist nicht mehr die Mittelerde-Mittelalter-Atmosphäre

claims.claim: Literaturschock readers argued Tolkien's archaic language is used deliberately as a stylistic device, so modernisation destroys the novel, citing 'Chef' and an alleged 'beim Fundbüro' as anachronisms.
claims.source: Tolkiens Der Herr der Ringe — Carroux vs. Krege (Literaturschock forum)
claims.quote: altertümliche Sprache gezielt als Stilmittel verwendet wird

claims.claim: Redaktion42 holds that Carroux keeps elevated, formal dialogue across all characters while Krege's naturalistic hobbit speech brought jarring modern vocabulary, and that the 2012 edition struck out the first edition's sins.
claims.source: Welche Herr der Ringe-Übersetzung ist die beste? (redaktion42)
claims.quote: die Sünden der ersten Übersetzung herausgestrichen

claims.claim: The Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft states Carroux's translation is the more popular among many Tolkien fans, and Klett-Cotta reissued it in a 2019 boxed set.
claims.source: Drei Mal Carroux im Schuber (Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft)

claims.claim: Twenty years after Krege the two translations still split German fans like almost no other topic, per the DTG's 2021 panel announcement.
claims.source: 20 Jahre nach Krege: Was taugen die deutschen Übersetzungen? (Deutsche Tolkien Gesellschaft)
claims.quote: spalten die Fans wie kaum ein anderes Thema

claims.claim: Krege criticised Carroux for using a similar linguistic style for the speech of both elves and hobbits despite the marked differences in the original.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: similar linguistic style for the speech of both elves and hobbits

claims.claim: Domènech's Spanish rendered working-class hobbits in grammatically correct Spanish, losing Tolkien's double negatives, altered agreement and subject duplication.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Tolkien's scheme maps Modern English to Westron, Old English to Rohirric and Old Norse to Dale, and Honegger suggests leaving Old English passages untranslated is probably best.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.feature: nomenclature not to be translated freely
claims.claim: Tolkien objected as strongly as possible to free translation of his nomenclature, writing the Guide after the Dutch and Swedish versions.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Tolkien called Bilbo's wealth 'a legend' and Ohlmarks added that his travels were legendary too, an instance of embroidering every description.
claims.source: Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Tolkien's archaic fronting ('Weapons they have laid at your doors') cannot be done in French and is unmarked in German, so its archaic effect is lost in translation.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors

claims.claim: Gollum's non-standard syntax and plurals like 'pocketses' resist translation; Ledoux's French diminishes both Gollum's and the Gaffer's peculiarities.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Livnit's Hebrew used a high Biblical register, and Lottem's revision mixed in technical modern Hebrew to an odd result.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.feature: register borrowed from a native genre
claims.claim: The Ding et al. Chinese version sounds like traditional wuxia fiction, while Chu produced a more popular version.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Parcerisas deliberately larded his Catalan Hobbit with learned or slightly archaic forms for school readers, gave the southern Men (Boromir, Faramir) dialect traits, and made the orcs' speech as broken as possible.
claims.source: Francesc Parcerisas, 'Traduir J. R. R. Tolkien' (Traducció literària, URV 2018)

claims.claim: Parcerisas notes the German case is the inverse of the Swedish: the first (Carroux) enjoys more prestige than the 2000 retranslation.
claims.source: Francesc Parcerisas, 'Traduir J. R. R. Tolkien' (Traducció literària, URV 2018)

claims.claim: Ohlmarks shifted Tolkien's simple language into hyperbolic, high-faluting expressions, adding words and long paraphrases throughout.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Ohlmarks claimed he had produced an interpretation of Tolkien, not a straight translation, and refused revision.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: an interpretation of Tolkien, not a straight translation

claims.claim: Andersson's prose matched Tolkien's laconic tone, using 24 words where Ohlmarks used 42 in one sampled sentence.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Critics of the 2005 version called it readable, even and largely correct, with prose following the original's fluent style very closely.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: readable, even and in large part correct

claims.claim: Ohlmarks's interpretive names include Vattnadal (confusing 'riven' with 'river'), Lavskägge (reading 'beam' as light) and Björnavad (from 'Bruin').
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Tolkien found Ohlmarks a conceited person and his version even worse than the Dutch, and called the nine-page list of altered names both puzzling and irritating.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: One reviewer conceded Ohlmarks's 'Vidstige' even outdoes the original's 'Strider'.
claims.source: Translation of The Lord of the Rings into Swedish (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Tolkien's Guide to the Names was produced in response to Ohlmarks, and Ohlmarks later turned hostile, publishing Tolkien and Black Magic in 1982.
claims.source: Åke Ohlmarks (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Andreas Brunner (2004) wrote that Ohlmarks added adjectives and spruced up dialogue, producing a delightful but quite different book.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Leif Jacobsen documented padding such as 'six meals a day' becoming 'sex vällagade måltider om dagen'.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Ohlmarks stated in 1978 that he rewrote after a plain draft to make the world feel ancient and distant from England.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Malte Persson found the Ohlmarks text packed with misunderstandings, misreadings, inconsistencies and arbitrary additions, including Merry credited with the Witch-king's death-blow and two names for the Prancing Pony.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Henrik Williams argued Andersson's 'Min dyrgrip' for 'precious' is lexically correct but loses the corrupting allure that Ohlmarks's 'älskade' caught.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Petter Lindgren expressed nostalgia for Ohlmarks's almost comically elaborate phrasing against Andersson's terse rendering.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Stefan Spjuth found 'Möcklegräva' for Michel Delving sounded like a place from Swedish MAD magazine.
claims.source: Översättning av Sagan om ringen till svenska (sv.wikipedia)

claims.claim: Strömbom found the narrator's voice completely changed in the new translation, so that it was practically a question of two different works.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: praktiskt taget var fråga om två olika verk

claims.claim: In the prologue's first sentence Tolkien and Andersson use simple language while Ohlmarks does not, turning 'a little' into 'en någorlunda klar bild av' against Andersson's 'litet'.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)

claims.claim: Ohlmarks's sentences are as a rule longer and more complex than the original's, with a somewhat higher stylistic value where Tolkien's word choice is simple and open.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)

claims.claim: Ohlmarks turns 'the pale king' into 'den dödsbleke konungen' and 'bathed Frodo's shoulder' into a bathing 'med dekokten', consistently seeking more drama than the original.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)

claims.claim: In 'Flight to the Ford' Ohlmarks's 'tröttnade aldrig på att inskärpa vikten av' adds a frenzy absent from Tolkien's and Andersson's matter-of-fact statements.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)
claims.quote: tröttnade aldrig på att inskärpa vikten av

claims.claim: Strömbom suggests Andersson sometimes cultivates a style even somewhat simpler than Tolkien's.
claims.source: Charlotte Strömbom, 'God åkermark eller fet och fruktbar mylla?' (Vetsaga)

claims.claim: The Tolkiens Arda reviewer holds that ornate language gets in the way of the story and that Andersson is more faithful to the English original than Ohlmarks, who added editorial glosses such as 'originell lustigkurre' at Bilbo's party.
claims.source: Recensionen: Ringarnas herre (Tolkiens Arda)

claims.claim: Andersson said the heroic register, especially in Book V, was the hardest to translate, and that names allow no room to manoeuvre.
claims.source: Intervju: Erik Andersson — om Ringens brödraskap (Tolkiens Arda)
claims.quote: Det finns inget svängrum i ett namn

claims.claim: Andersson observed the book starts out as a children's book and moves into a more sinister mode, and that Aragorn's speech varies between ranger and king.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien — Erik Andersson interview (TheOneRing.net, 2004)
claims.quote: starts out as a children's book

claims.claim: Andersson called Ohlmarks's version excellent as a creation in its own right even if it does not always follow Tolkien.
claims.source: Translating Tolkien — Erik Andersson interview (TheOneRing.net, 2004)
claims.quote: As a creation in its own right it is excellent

claims.claim: The Tolkien på svenska essay charges that Andersson tones down the differences between the original's varieties of language, removes Sam's courteous address, lacks the ear for poetry, and that his small deviations all run in the same direction.
claims.source: Om Erik Anderssons översättning (Tolkien på svenska)

claims.claim: The same essay insists that in Tolkien's text how something is said matters as much as what is said.
claims.source: Om Erik Anderssons översättning (Tolkien på svenska)

claims.claim: Johan Groth finds Andersson reduces 'pages', 'reader' and 'discover' to 'den', 'man' and 'få reda på', while Ohlmarks's showy style grows beyond all bounds.
claims.source: Ringarna herre (igen) samt några synpunkter på Åke Ohlmarks (Johan Groth)

claims.claim: Andersson's diary records his fear of the 'anglicism ghost' and his search for names like 'Riftedal' that keep the English sound while reading as Swedish.
claims.source: Utdrag ur Översättarens anmärkningar (Erik Andersson diary excerpts)

claims.claim: Shippey's afterword considers Tolkien's imitators and what they do not imitate, notably language-building and interlaced storylines.
claims.source: T.A. Shippey — J.R.R. Tolkien: Author of the Century (Falling Letters review)

claims.claim: Shippey holds that no modern writer of fantasy has managed to escape the mark of Tolkien.
claims.source: J. R. R. Tolkien: Author of the Century (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Shippey noted The Sword of Shannara's dogged adherence to Tolkien with point-for-point analogues (Sauron to Brona, Gandalf to Allanon, hobbits to Shea and Flick).
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Lin Carter wrote that Brooks was not trying to imitate Tolkien's prose but to steal his story line and cast, calling it the most cold-blooded complete rip-off of another book.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: wasn't trying to imitate Tolkien's prose

claims.claim: Brian Attebery called The Sword of Shannara undigested Tolkien with especially blatant correspondences, while Choice praised it as exceptionally well-written and very readable.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Brooks acknowledged heavy Tolkien influence in his first novel and said he then adopted a popular-fiction approach rather than an academic tone.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Contemporary critics of Shannara focused almost exclusively on plot and world-building parallels rather than prose, with Choice calling it exceptionally well-written.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara: The Critics Fifty Years Later (Dark Worlds Quarterly)

claims.claim: Vredenburgh judges that Shannara talks when it should at least be trying to sing, is bereft of atmosphere, and follows Tolkien's story architecture rather than his prose.
claims.source: Half a Century of Reading Tolkien, Part Seven: The Sword of Shannara (Black Gate)
claims.quote: talks when it should at least be trying to sing

claims.claim: Tom Simon finds Brooks's prose stilted and turgid, alternating between expository lumps and expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue, with names uniformly slipshod.
claims.source: 1977: Lord of the Rinky-dink (Tom Simon, Bondwine)
claims.quote: expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue

claims.claim: Simon cites Shippey's point that readers hungry for heroic fantasy would take any substitute no matter how diluted, and del Rey's targeting of young readers least likely to notice the writing.
claims.source: 1977: Lord of the Rinky-dink (Tom Simon, Bondwine)
claims.quote: take any substitute, no matter how diluted

claims.claim: The Big Bad Book Blog counts adjectives and adverbs at 21% of words in a sample passage, calls the prose wooden yet lightweight, and notes dialogue tags like 'blazed up angrily' replacing 'said'.
claims.source: The Sword of Shannara by Terry Brooks (The Big Bad Book Blog)

claims.claim: Dial H For Houston contrasts Tolkien's invented languages with Brooks naming a corner of the map after a direction, and calls the prose flat.
claims.source: Book Review: Terry Brooks' The Sword of Shannara (Dial H For Houston)

claims.claim: Attebery said Shannara tries to evoke wonder without engaging the mind or emotions, reducing Tolkien to a bare formula; Jane Yolen saw derivative fantasy sinking into pastel unicorns and coy talking swords.
claims.source: Tolkien's impact on fantasy (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Critics stress that Tolkien's impression of depth and historical background is what formulaic followers fail to replicate.
claims.source: Tolkien's impact on fantasy (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Le Guin characterised Tolkien's prose as quieter English of simple timelessness with sobriety, wit and force, ranging easily from the commonplace to the stately and able to slide into metrical poetry.
claims.source: It's intentional (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2011)

claims.claim: Tolkien defended Théoden's archaic speech on the ground that modern dialogue would create an insincerity of thought and a disunion of word and meaning, and gave Elrond the most archaisms as the eldest speaker.
claims.source: It's intentional (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2011)
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Le Guin faulted Zelazny and Leiber for talking colloquial American English when humour is intended and reverting to old formal usages at earnest moments.
claims.source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)
claims.quote: at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages

claims.claim: Le Guin's test is to change a passage's names to mundane ones and see whether it still reads as fantasy; Kurtz's Deryni fails as fancy dress.
claims.source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)

claims.claim: Le Guin warned against forced archaic language as a crutch, praising Tolkien's plain clear English, concrete vocabulary that avoids 'ichor', and the principle that the style is the book.
claims.source: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie to The Witcher (Nick Gibney)

claims.claim: Applying Le Guin, TheOneRing.net found The Rings of Power's 'Okay', 'like', 'Nah', 'Yeah' and 'conflicted' expose modern minds, while its over-correction lapses into fortune-cookie 'High Aphorism'.
claims.source: From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie (TheOneRing.net, 2022)

claims.claim: Le Guin's essay separates the risky inner lands of Elfland from banal imitation that is the outside world in disguise, and Beagle called it the definitive piece on fantasy.
claims.source: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Brennan observes writers sticking '-st' on every second-person verb and '-th' on every third-person one, and warns archaic grammar is very easily overused.
claims.source: Archaic Grammar (Marie Brennan, Swan Tower)

claims.claim: Epic fantasy's archaisms fall into be-perfects ('Winter is come'), be- prefixes, hither/thither, thou/thee, postposed modifiers and do-less imperatives, used to suggest a whole past speech community.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)

claims.claim: A commenter notes the Nazgûl uses thee/thou while Éowyn answers in modern 'you', and that Tolkien was very deliberate about when he used 'thou'.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
claims.quote: very deliberate about when he used 'thou'

claims.claim: 'From whence it came' is a common archaism error because 'whence' already contains 'from'.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)

claims.claim: Bored of the Rings steps through the prologue, the map and the main text in turn, substituting brand names (Moxie and Pepsi, Serutan) for Tolkien's invented terms.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The parody replaces Tolkien's Sindarin hymn with nonsense modern references ('Unicef clearasil') and parodies the Watcher in the Water as a thesaurus-monster.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: David Bratman remarked that the parodists wrought better than they knew, since Tolkien's drafts came close to writing the parody version of his own novel before he avoided it.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: David Barnett judged the parody shows respect and affection for the source despite its crudity.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The Phuulish Fellow review finds the parody works best when it references Tolkien's own recognisable words and phrases, includes copious inserted verse, and that Tolkien's Party speech is actually funnier than the parody.
claims.source: Review: Bored of the Rings (1969) (A Phuulish Fellow)

claims.claim: My Tolkien Archive judges the parody mimics the forms (foreword, map, prologue) with lazy names, without genuine engagement with Tolkien's prose itself.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings: A Parody (My Tolkien Archive)

claims.claim: Pechey Ponderings notes the parody's embedded songs are well-crafted and its foreword disclaims any attempt to fill Tolkien's shoes.
claims.source: Bored of the Rings review (Pechey Ponderings)

claims.claim: The Tough Guide's Stew entry mocks stew as the universal fantasy meal even though it takes forty times as long to prepare as steak.
claims.source: The DWJ Project: Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Swan Tower)
claims.quote: forty times as long to prepare as steak

claims.claim: The Guide observes that few Fantasyland names are considered complete unless interrupted by an apostrophe nobody knows how to pronounce.
claims.source: The Tough Guide To Fantasyland — Review (HearWriteNow)
claims.quote: complete unless interrupted by an apostrophe

claims.claim: Shalizi's review frames the Guide as an attack on fifty years of trilogies that are debased versions of The Lord of the Rings, which Jones calls elf operas.
claims.source: Diana Wynne Jones, The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Cosma Shalizi review)

claims.claim: The English Student review reads entries from 'Stew' to 'Reek of Wrongness' as exposing a tour of something made just strange enough to fascinate, with Tolkien as the deeply English conservative template.
claims.source: Review: The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (The English Student)
claims.quote: made just strange enough to fascinate

claims.claim: Wikipedia describes the Guide's tone as either thinly veiled criticism of the genre's derivative nature or an affectionate study.
claims.source: The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Sibley and Bakewell's script incorporated many sections of dialogue lifted directly from the book, such as the Window on the West conversations.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: many sections of dialogue lifted directly

claims.claim: Sibley preferred removing minor characters entirely to the alternative, which would have been to fabricate dialogue for them.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The adaptation radically restructured books 3-6, flattening Tolkien's interlacing into the Appendix chronology and splicing Frodo and Sam's journey with events in the West.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Christopher Tolkien approved the scripts and recorded a cassette of correct pronunciations of Middle-earth names for the cast.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Rosebury praised the dialogue delivery and Woodthorpe's Gollum but found the skilful abridgement subtly reshaped Tolkien's text in the direction of an adventure story.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: in the direction of an adventure story

claims.claim: Christina Scull called it a masterly adaptation that caught the spirit of the books, found the alliterative-verse handling of the Pelennor a brilliant idea, and contrasted its characters as in the book with the films' weakening of almost all the characters.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1981 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The Tolkien Library review states Tolkien's language is left intact in the mouths of the proper characters, delivered with highly trained diction that keeps the subtle differences in accents of the book.
claims.source: Review: The BBC Lord of the Rings Dramatization (Tolkien Library)
claims.quote: left intact in the mouths of the proper characters

claims.claim: The production set many poems to music, with Bill Nighy singing the fall of Gil-galad and Bilbo's Last Song and Douglas Livingstone reciting the Khazad-dûm poem.
claims.source: Review: The BBC Lord of the Rings Dramatization (Tolkien Library)

claims.claim: Brunstrom hears Robert Stephens's Prancing-Pony rusticity remain a leitmotif against his later kingly majesty, and notes Sibley keeps as much of Tolkien's dialogue as possible.
claims.source: The 1981 BBC Lord of the Rings radio adaptation reviewed (Conrad Brunstrom)

claims.claim: To spare the narrator, descriptions were transferred into dialogue, so that Sam is awkwardly forced to narrate his Shelob fight in real time.
claims.source: The 1981 BBC Lord of the Rings radio adaptation reviewed (Conrad Brunstrom)

claims.claim: The Pelennor Fields sequence interweaves battle dialogue between verses of a Rohan lay written afterwards.
claims.source: The 1981 BBC Lord of the Rings radio adaptation reviewed (Conrad Brunstrom)

claims.claim: Brundige reports Sibley and Bakewell use Tolkien's words almost exclusively except for stage directions, and shun flashback and the narrator's voice as much as possible.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)

claims.claim: For the Pelennor the adapters combed Tolkien's prose and recast lines of it in metre and alliteration as extra ballad stanzas, e.g. 'crashed to the ground with the king crushed beneath him'.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: with the king crushed beneath him

claims.claim: Brundige praises a Faramir whose courtly speech shows his quality and an Aragorn whose manner of speech is altered not a jot, as proof that Tolkien's heroes can sound like flesh-and-blood people.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: manner of speech altered not a jot

claims.claim: Brundige argues that language is part of what makes the book stand out and radio gives it full wings to fly.
claims.source: The BBC Radio Play of LOTR — a Fan's Review (Ellen Brundige, istad.org)
claims.quote: radio gives it full wings to fly

claims.claim: Sibley (2019) said he used a narrator because it lets you capture the authorial voice of the book, convey place and passing time, and move across scenes when the Fellowship splits.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: capture the authorial voice of the book

claims.claim: Contains Moderate Peril notes great care was taken with pronunciation and with dialogue spoken in Elvish and the Black Speech, and that characterisations and dialogue were extremely well realised.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings — BBC Radio Adaptation (1981) (Contains Moderate Peril)
claims.quote: the delivery of dialogue spoken in Elvish

claims.claim: Sibley's own page credits Gerard Murphy with the series' strong narrative voice, notes Christopher Tolkien's pronunciation cassette, and concedes that Tolkien's interlaced chronology could not be applied to a dramatic presentation.
claims.source: Brian Sibley: The Works — The Lord of the Rings (BBC Radio 1981)

claims.claim: Tolkien told Tiller in 1956 that dramatisation results in too great an emphasis on dialogue, mostly with its setting removed.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)
claims.quote: too great an emphasis on dialogue

claims.claim: In 1957 Tolkien wrote he would find vulgarisation less painful than the sillification achieved by the BBC.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Series One, which cut scenes, was welcomed (appreciation 64/100); Series Two, which compressed them, was heard as a footling and ridiculous-sounding adventure story.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.feature: dialogue preserved as far as possible
claims.claim: Tiller promised Tolkien that the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible, with a narrator linking scenes and cutting preferred to summarising.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: Tiller admitted that a great deal of the flavour of the work had been lost through telescoping incidents, and Tolkien replied he did not think more could have been done in the time.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: a great deal of the flavour

claims.claim: Tolkien rejected the expectation that hobbits should pipe and squeak, asking why tones should rise with fall in stature, and judged the Elves managed excellently, the Council of Elrond masterly, and Bilbo bored.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: Why should tones rise with fall in stature?

claims.claim: Tolkien liked Glóin's accent but found it heavily laid on, noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively with a uvular back R.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: A 1955 review held that Tolkien's relaxed, vivid and masculine style with its rich coinages adapted naturally to radio and held attention even when expository.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: Listeners to the compressed Series Two called it an absolute ruin and a farce whose ignominious compression produced a juvenile adventure story.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story

claims.claim: Tolkien described Norman Shelley's Bombadil as dreadful and the announcer's misdescription of Goldberry and Willowman as worse still (Letters 175, 176, 198).
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: The 1979 Mind's Eye version removed much back history and expository narration and, with lines recorded separately, produced curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue and frequent mispronunciations.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings — The Mind's Eye Radio Adaptation (1979) (Contains Moderate Peril)

claims.claim: Wikipedia notes the Virginia theatre players of the 1979 adaptation had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places, though the version kept Tom Bombadil.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1979 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The 2017 Tolkien: Medieval and Modern post argues Jackson replaced Tolkien's speech-register distinctions (rustic hobbits, more antique Gondor and Rohan) with visual accents, turning Gandalf's conditional syntax into the flat 'The Ring is altogether evil'.
claims.source: How Peter Jackson's Movies Fail to Adapt Tolkien's Style (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2017)

claims.claim: The same post holds that Jackson introduces ironic mockery of characters, a mode Tolkien never uses, and cuts nearly all verse that distinguished the peoples.
claims.source: How Peter Jackson's Movies Fail to Adapt Tolkien's Style (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2017)

claims.claim: Croft's 'Mithril Coats and Tin Ears' argues Jackson and Zimmerman flattened Tolkien's characters, dialogue and plot and showed too much too soon.
claims.source: Tolkien on Film (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann's corpus study shows Aragorn archaic with inversions, Sam colloquial and politely hedged, Gandalf plain and commanding, Legolas and Gimli proverbial, and Gollum an idiolect of obsessive repetition and minimal syntax.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Walker finds Tolkien uses few actually archaic words yet achieves a nostalgic, maybe even archaic essence through words like 'deem', 'moot', 'wight' and 'westering'.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Turner shows Tolkien's paratactic 'and'-linked sentences at key moments create an impression of exalted register through biblical association without archaic vocabulary.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Vaninskaya observes the Orcs speak the most modern idiom in the book, the clipped language of army dispatches and bureaucrats.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The Riders of Rohan receive the fullest archaic treatment, with rescued Old English words such as éored, dwimmerlaik and mearas and actual Old English phrases.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The Silmarillion documents events briefly as if in annals rather than describing persons, giving what Shippey calls more rarefied air.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings contains 45-50 embedded stories told by 23 characters; about half the novel is dialogue, poetry or character-narrated tales and 85% of the narrative is from a Hobbit perspective.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Stimpson accused Tolkien of shunning ordinary diction and Moorcock called the style comforting and unchallenging, charges Rosebury refuted by showing plain modern English.
claims.source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Rosebury shows Tolkien favours familiar phrasal verbs such as 'have on' and 'get off' over the more literary 'wear' and 'dismount'.
claims.source: Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon (Wikipedia)
